Q4430774.summary: Christ sits frontally on a high carved throne, IC XC beside his haloed head, holding an open Gospel book in his left hand; the fingers of his right hand point to its Greek text, 'I am the light of the world'. His robes are worked all over with gold. The icon came from Saint Sophia in Novgorod, and although its surface is a later repainting, it preserves an unusual 11th-century image of Christ the Teacher.
facts: According to Russian sources, Kirill Ulanov, the tsar's icon painter, repainted the icon almost entirely in 1700; nothing visible remains of the 11th-century painting, though he kept the old composition.
The icon came from Saint Sophia Cathedral in Novgorod; Ivan the Terrible brought it to Moscow in 1570, and Patriarch Nikon placed it in the iconostasis of the Kremlin's Dormition Cathedral in 1655.
Its name comes from a solid silver-gilt cover (riza) that once covered it and is now lost.

links.label: Wikipedia (fr): Le Sauveur à la riza d'or

Q4430774.notes: The original is 11th century (probably c. 1050), but the paint surface seen today dates from 1700 (the Commons file says 1699). y is kept at 1050 for the composition. The Commons description gives the size as 236 × 147 cm.

cur:catacombs-louvre-castelnau-de-guers-.summary: Panels of vine scrolls, flowers and fruit alternate with three framed figures: at the centre Christ, flanked by two apostles. The flat, ornamental carving shows how the Christian sarcophagus survived into the 6th century in Gaul, with Christ still at the centre of the tomb.
facts: The Louvre catalogue entry recorded on Commons gives its size as 49 × 201 × 70 cm and its provenance as Castelnau-de-Guers (Hérault).
It has been exhibited at the Louvre-Lens in the 'Galerie du Temps'.

cur:monumental-san-agony-in-garden.summary: Among the olive trees of Gethsemane, the bearded Christ stands upright with arms raised in prayer, while below him the disciples sit and sleep in two groups, wrapped in white. The composition, with Christ towering over his sleeping companions, is among the earliest monumental images of the Agony in the Garden.
facts: On the south wall the thirteen Passion and Resurrection scenes show Christ bearded; the cycle omits both the Flagellation and the Crucifixion.
The scenes were not arranged in biblical order but are thought to follow the Gospel readings of the Lenten liturgy in Theodoric's palace church.

UNESCO: Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna

met:446060.summary: Cut from a thin piece of mother-of-pearl only 3 cm high and pierced at the top for suspension, this small cross is incised with the figure of the crucified Christ, his arms stretched along the crossbar and his body clothed in a long garment. The simple, lively lines make it a personal devotional pendant, worn by an Egyptian Christian as a sign of faith in the One who died on the cross.
facts: The Met attributes it to Egypt and gives a very broad date range, 3rd–12th century, reflecting how difficult such small devotional objects are to date.
met:446060.notes: Acc. 10.130.1154, Gift of Helen Miller Gould, 1910. The Met date of 3rd–12th century means its placement in the 7th century (y 700) is arbitrary; a crucified Christ wearing a long garment would be consistent with an early date but this is not confirmed. Small incised marks above the figure are not legible in the photograph.

Q116411335.summary: This small bronze pectoral cross, made of two hinged halves to hold a relic, is engraved on one face with the Virgin, marked by the letters for 'Mother of God', and on the other with a simply incised standing figure of Christ. Crosses like this were worn by ordinary believers, who carried close to the heart both the sign of Christ's cross and a fragment of holy matter.
facts: The Met explains that such crosses were made of two crosses hinged at the bottom, enclosing a hollow space for a relic.
The many surviving copper-alloy examples suggest they usually held secondary relics, such as earth from a holy site or cloth touched to a saint's body, rather than relics of the True Cross.
Q116411335.notes: The primary image shows the Virgin's face; Christ is on the reverse (Met additional image DP-14824-005). The Met's date range is very broad (9th–13th century); y 1050 is a midpoint.

wga:m/master/zunk_ge/zunk_ge6/05cross1.summary: This over-life-size walnut figure of the dead Christ survives as a torso, with one arm broken away and the cross itself lost. His head sinks onto his shoulder, his eyes are closed, and his finely grooved hair and beard frame a face of quiet, solemn stillness, while a long loincloth falls in heavy folds to his knees. Carved for the church of St. Georg in Cologne, it is one of the great early monumental crucifixes of the German Romanesque.
facts: It comes from the church of St. Georg in Cologne, rebuilt under Archbishop Anno II (1056–1075); a copy now hangs in the choir there, while the original torso is kept in the Museum Schnütgen.
The figure is carved from walnut and is about 196 cm high.
wga:m/master/zunk_ge/zunk_ge6/05cross1.notes: German Wikipedia dates the original to 1067; WGA gives c. 1070.
